# CHAPTER 16

## Running the Governance

> *A pattern is the depiction of the fundamental nature of an object, it is what remains of an object’s form after all that is unnecessary had been removed.*
>
> *Soetsu Yanagi, The Beauty of Everyday Things*

**Running the governance is not the same as operating it. Running it means deciding whether and how the enterprise can act in the first place, and keeping that decision true as the systems change. No single function does this. Chapter 7 stated one allocation of the named human: Final Liability attaches to the accountable executive named per deployment; the General Counsel owns the authority design; engineering owns enforcement and evidence; internal audit assures the join; and the management body owns the risk appetite. This chapter sets out how that allocation runs.**

Earlier chapters in Part III set out the structural conditions that make governance hard at machine speed. Chapter 14 described the Three Lines and the trust boundary. Chapter 15 described what principal-agent risk looks like when agents act faster than principals can supervise. This chapter takes the next step. It describes what each of the five owners must do for the governance to run, what each produces and where each part fails if another owner tries to carry it.

## Running Is Not the Same as Operating

The verb to run is used in many ways inside organizations. A business unit runs its operations. A technology function runs its systems. A finance function runs its books. A compliance function runs its program. Each of these uses the verb to mean something specific to the function: to operate the assigned activity to a defined standard, on a defined cadence, with defined accountability for defined outputs.

Running the governance means something different. The governance is not an operation. It is the architecture that determines what the operations are permitted and capable of doing: which controls exist, which thresholds trigger which escalations, which actions require which approvals, which outcomes require which evidence and which exceptions break the architecture badly enough to warrant a redesign.

The distinction matters because organizations frequently misunderstand it. A governance, risk management and compliance function that operates the controls, processes the exceptions, signs off the filings and produces the artifacts is performing operational work. The work is necessary. It is not running the governance. A function that only operates the controls inherits a design it did not author and cannot defend when the design fails. It processes the exceptions but does not own the threshold. It approves the actions but does not own the criteria. When the consequence arrives, it cannot explain the design, because the design was not its own.

Strong governance makes ownership explicit. Every part of the architecture has an owner, the owners are named before the system runs and the joins between their parts are tested. That is what the allocation is for.

## The Five Owners

**The management body owns the risk appetite.** It decides what kinds and levels of AI-related risk the organization will accept: which uses are out of bounds, what residual risk is tolerable for which classes of system and, as Chapter 14 sets out, the ratio of agents to human oversight the organization is prepared to govern with systems it will stand behind. The appetite is a decision made in advance and recorded. It is not a number discovered after an incident. A deployment outside the appetite cannot be signed for by anyone below the management body, however complete its record.

**The accountable executive carries Final Liability for the deployment.** One executive is named for each deployment, by role and incumbent, before the system runs. The executive owns the business outcome the system serves and holds the three attributes the doctrine requires: decision rights over the deployment, oversight of how it performs and the power to intervene, up to stopping it. The executive signs for the deployment. The signature says that the four components of Chapter 7 are present and current for this system: the named human, the Informed Intent record, the capability to stop and the evidence pipeline. Where a later question asks who signed for this, this is the name.

**The General Counsel owns the authority design.** Corporate authority is a legal construct. It derives from the corporate form, the board’s resolutions, the delegations of authority, the agency relationships and the contracts that bind the entity to its counterparties. The General Counsel designs who may sign for a deployment, on what evidence, with what stop authority and against which legal, regulatory and contractual exposures. The General Counsel also holds the question of which risks are unacceptable as a matter of law, regulation, contract or fiduciary obligation, whatever the risk register says, and which consequences cannot be transferred by insurance or indemnity. The General Counsel signs for the design. It does not sign for each deployment inside it, and it cannot sign on the executive’s behalf.

**Engineering owns enforcement and evidence.** A boundary stated in a policy and not enforced in the system is a hope. Engineering builds the controls that hold the system inside its authorized boundary: credential scope, tool permissions, human gates, the pause and the rollback. It builds the pipeline that records what the system did, in a form the system generating it cannot modify. Engineering is also where the design meets reality, because only engineering knows where each prohibited condition is actually enforced: outside the model, by credential scope, at a human gate or by instruction only. An enforcement point that exists only as an instruction to the model is recorded as such, so that the executive signing for the deployment knows what the boundary rests on.

**Internal audit assures the join.** The authority as designed, the enforcement as built and the evidence as recorded are three artifacts produced by three owners. Governance exists only where they describe the same system. Internal audit tests that they do, for the deployment as it actually runs, and reports to the management body on whether the allocation is working. It does not design the authority, build the controls or sign for the deployment. Its independence from all three is what makes its assurance worth having.

## Why No Single Function Runs It

Four elements must be bound together to produce governance that can be defended later: authority, risk, evidence and consequence. Authority without evidence cannot be defended. Risk without consequence is a notional exposure. Evidence without authority is a record of unauthorized action. Consequence without risk identification is an unprepared loss.

Earlier versions of this book argued that the General Counsel alone connects all four. It does not. The General Counsel designs authority and holds the legal view of risk and consequence, but it does not build the enforcement or produce the evidence, and it does not own the business outcome that gives the deployment its purpose. A Chief AI Officer or a Chief Technology Officer has technical reach but does not bind the entity. A Chief Risk Officer has the perspective on risk but does not own the evidence architecture. An AI ethics committee deliberates but cannot be an owner. A cross-functional steering group distributes the work in a way that makes the join nobody’s responsibility.

The answer is not a better candidate for the single seat. It is the allocation. Each element has an owner who can actually produce it, the owners are named in advance and the join is assured by a function independent of all of them. The proposals to give AI governance wholly to one function, the General Counsel included, are proposals to let one owner carry a part it cannot produce.

This is not a demotion of the General Counsel. The authority design is the part every other owner works inside. An executive cannot sign for a deployment under an authority nobody designed. Engineering cannot enforce a boundary nobody authorized. Internal audit cannot assure a join that has no specification. The General Counsel leads the design because the design comes first.

## The Design Function

Designing the authority is not a one-time event. It is an ongoing discipline. The design must adapt to new technologies, new regulations, new business activities, new contractual arrangements, new vendor relationships and new operational realities. Each change exposes the design to a question the previous version did not answer.

In the agentic era, that discipline has accelerated. New deployments, model versions, use cases, agent configurations, data flows and automated decisions present design questions that must be answered before the deployment proceeds, not after. The General Counsel’s design work must therefore run at the cadence of deployment, not at the quarterly or semi-annual rhythm governance functions traditionally adopted. Engineering’s enforcement work must keep pace with it, because a revised authority that engineering has not yet enforced is a revision on paper.

This is hard. It requires the General Counsel to be positioned at the deployment decision point, with the standing to block a deployment the design has not yet accommodated and the capacity to revise the design quickly enough that the blocks do not become bottlenecks. Most General Counsel functions today sit downstream of deployment decisions, with authority to advise but not to block. The functions that move upstream, into the design conversation, will be running their part of the governance. The functions that stay downstream will be documenting the consequences of designs they did not author.

## What Running the Governance Looks Like

In operational terms, running the governance produces four outputs, each with an owner.

The first is the architecture itself: the documented design that specifies which actions require which authorities, which authorities can be exercised by which roles, which evidence each authorization must produce, which controls operate at each gate and which conditions trigger which escalations. The General Counsel owns the design. Engineering owns the record of where each control is enforced.

The second is the live record of where the architecture has been tested and how it performed. Every material decision, every refused deployment, every triggered escalation, every incident and every regulatory inquiry is data about the architecture. Engineering maintains the record. The accountable executives use it to know whether what they signed for is still true.

The third is the change log: the documented sequence of changes to the design and to its enforcement, with the reason for each change, the date of effect, the impacted areas and the verification that the change has propagated. Architectures without change logs become folklore. The General Counsel keeps the log for the design; engineering keeps it for enforcement; internal audit reconciles the two.

The fourth is readiness for the asking. At any point, a regulator, an auditor, a litigant, a Client, an investor or a board member may ask: who signed for this, under what authority, on what evidence and within what appetite? The accountable executive answers for the deployment. The General Counsel answers for the design. Internal audit answers for whether the two match the system as it runs. The asking does not require preparation, because the preparation has been continuous.

These outputs are not glamorous. They are also rare. Most enterprises today do not have them in the form the AI era requires. The architecture exists in fragments, the live record is scattered across functions, the change log does not exist as a discrete artifact and the readiness for the asking is constructed after the asking has occurred.

## What This Chapter Has Done

The chapter has distinguished running the governance from operating it and set out how the allocation stated in Chapter 7 runs: the management body owns the risk appetite; the accountable executive named per deployment carries Final Liability; the General Counsel owns the authority design; engineering owns enforcement and evidence; and internal audit assures the join.

The chapter has withdrawn the claim that one function, the General Counsel included, can connect authority, risk, evidence and consequence alone, and replaced it with the allocation.

The chapter has named the four outputs that running the governance produces and the owner of each.

**Final Liability rests with the Human.**
